const draft = `# Elm Quay brings trial reports into one log

Elm Quay Housing tested a shared repair log in two buildings. This account, published by supplier Svale Systems, follows the team's choices, the limits of its trial figures, and the maintenance supervisor's assessment of what to allow for next time.

By Thomas Barregren

Telephone reports and emails were stored separately at Elm Quay Housing, which manages 640 apartments. In September 2025, its maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log so staff on different shifts could see the same information.

## The team keeps telephone reporting open

The team chose Svale Systems after testing whether the log could show the status of each repair. Residents could still report repairs by telephone. Svale configured the log and trained six staff during two sessions.

Maintenance supervisor Maya Lind explained the aim in an email interview: “We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done. The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log.”

Lind also recalled the setup work: “We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts.”

## The trial note limits the comparison

The trial lasted eight weeks. Elm Quay's internal trial note, dated December 4, 2025, says that 31 repair reports were entered. The note excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial.

Median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial, compared with three in the preceding eight-week period. The periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software.

There were no cost, resident-satisfaction, or completion-time measurements. Lind's appraisal was separate from those figures: “I would choose to do the trial again. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation.”

## Readers can consult the implementation checklist

The team will decide on expansion after checking how the categories work for larger repairs; the trial has not yet expanded. For operations managers considering their own setup, the supplied next step is to [read Svale's implementation checklist](https://example.invalid/svale/checklist).
`;
store("write_draft", draft);

cmd: "python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
report = r'''# Source and quotation comparison 1

Compared the complete source/brief in `source.md` with the complete current `draft.md`. Both texts were read in full. This comparison covers source support, attribution, qualifications, pronoun information, and quotation fidelity. It does not cover general editing or mechanics. Source and draft are English; quotations are untranslated. The supplied byline is authorized by the invocation and is not a source-support finding.

## Complete claim accounting

Each source excerpt below reproduces the source's words. Where surrounding qualifications affect a claim, they are included in its accounting. The draft's narrative present in its title/headings is read conventionally as a description of the historical case, not as an assertion that a new trial is occurring now.

| # | Draft passage | Source passage, in the source's own words | Comparison and disposition |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | “Elm Quay brings trial reports into one log” | “In September 2025 its own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings.” / “Elm Quay's internal trial note, 4 December 2025, says that 31 repair reports were entered.” | The title summarizes entry of trial reports into the shared log. It does not say all repair reports were entered, that every building participated, or that all reporting channels closed. A shared log and entry of reports support the title. | 2 | “Elm Quay Housing tested a shared repair log in two buildings.” | “In September 2025 its own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings.” / “The trial lasted eight weeks.” | The source describes a decision and a trial that occurred, supporting the draft's completed trial. “Tested” here means trialed; the draft does not suggest a supplier comparison or exhaustive evaluation. Supported. |

This does not claim independent publication. Supported. |
| 4 | “follows the team's choices, the limits of its trial figures, and the maintenance supervisor's assessment of what to allow for next time.” | “The maintenance team designed its categories and kept telephone reporting open for residents.” / “The periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software.” / “Customer interview with maintenance supervisor Maya Lind, complete usable quotations:” / “I would set that time aside before the next building starts.” / “I would choose to do the trial again. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation.” | This is an accurate description of the account's content. “Assessment of what to allow for next time” refers to the preparation reservations in the quotations. The team's decisions, the comparison's qualification, and the supervisor's role are all supported. |
| 5 | “By Thomas Barregren” | No source passage; the invoking user's identity was supplied separately. | Authorized contextual metadata. As instructed, its absence from the source is not a finding. |
| 6 | “Telephone reports and emails were stored separately at Elm Quay Housing” | “Previously telephone reports and emails were stored separately.” | The narrative places this in the prior arrangement, as the source does. No claim of continued separation after setup is added. Supported. |
| 7 | “which manages 640 apartments.” | “Elm Quay Housing manages 640 flats.” | Same entity, count, and housing units. In this English housing context, American English “apartments” names the units called “flats” in the source; no context-compatible distinction between these two uses changes the count or unit. Supported locale wording. |
| 8 | “In September 2025, its maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log” | “In September 2025 its own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings.” | Same actor, date, decision, and object. The two-building restriction is stated in the introduction and remains the scope of this trial. “Its maintenance team” preserves the source's ownership, including “own.” Supported. |
| 9 | “so staff on different shifts could see the same information.” | “The team wanted staff on different shifts to see the same information.” | “Decided ... so ... could” states the team's purpose. It does not state that all staff subsequently saw or used the same information. Purpose and intended beneficiaries are supported. |
| 10 | “The team keeps telephone reporting open” | “The maintenance team designed its categories and kept telephone reporting open for residents.” | The heading preserves the maintenance team's agency and the continued telephone channel. The narrative present does not claim a new present-day action. Supported. |
| 11 | “The team chose Svale Systems after testing whether the log could show the status of each repair.” | “It chose Svale Systems after testing whether the log could show the status of each repair. No comparison with another supplier is available.” | Exact selection criterion, sequence, and test question. “The team” resolves source “It” without changing its referent. The draft claims no comparison with competitors. Supported. |
| 12 | “Residents could still report repairs by telephone.” | “The maintenance team designed its categories and kept telephone reporting open for residents.” | Same continuing availability, beneficiary, and channel. “Could” does not assert use of the channel, a volume of calls, or successful resolution of them. Supported. |
| 13 | “Svale configured the log and trained six staff during two sessions.” | “Svale configured the log and trained six staff during two sessions.” | Verbatim factual claim, including provider, actions, staff count, and session count. Supported. |
| 14 | “Maintenance supervisor Maya Lind explained the aim in an email interview” | “Customer interview with maintenance supervisor Maya Lind, complete usable quotations:” / “All interviews occurred by email, and no physical scene, emotion or remembered dialogue is provided.” / “We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done. The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log.” | Name, role, interview medium, and the characterization as an explanation of the aim are supported. No scene, emotion, or recalled dialogue is added. |
| 15 | “We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done. The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log.” | “We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done. The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log.” | Verbatim complete supplied quotation. “Wanted” remains an intention. Customer ownership of the categories and supplier assistance remain distinct. No scope, certainty, voice, or attribution changes. Supported. |
| 16 | “Lind also described the setup work” | “We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts.” | The categories and initial entries are setup work in the supplied context. The description adds no quantified duration or attribution of delay. Supported. |
| 17 | “We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts.” | “We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts.” | Verbatim complete supplied quotation. | 18 | “The trial note limits the comparison” | “The periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software.” | The heading identifies the note's express qualification of the reported comparison. | 20 | “Elm Quay's internal trial note, dated December 4, 2025, says that 31 repair reports were entered.” | “Elm Quay's internal trial note, 4 December 2025, says that 31 repair reports were entered. It excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial.” | Same document, ownership, internal status, date, reported count, and entry event. American date order preserves the calendar date. The exclusions are stated in the next draft sentence. The draft attributes the number to the note and does not value it as high or low. Supported. |

The periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software.” | Same statistic, starting event, ending event, working-day unit, values, periods, and comparison. “Three” retains the unit and statistic from the first clause. No cause, tentative causal inference, or direction of workload difference is invented. Supported. |
| 24 | “There were no cost, resident-satisfaction, or completion-time measurements.” | “There are no cost, resident-satisfaction or completion-time measurements.” | The measurement categories are preserved, but the historical existential assertion differs from the source's present absence of measurements. See finding F1: the draft can be read as establishing that such measurements did not exist during the trial, beyond what the source establishes about their present availability. |
| 25 | “Lind's appraisal was separate from those figures” | “Lind did not recommend Svale to every housing company. Her final quotation is her actual, qualified assessment. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation.” | Verbatim complete supplied quotation. The speaker's conditional choice, her own report of benefit, plural beneficiary, and preparation reservation survive. The benefit is her attributed assessment, not an inferred measured saving or causal assignment-time result. Supported. |
| 27 | “Readers can consult the implementation checklist” | “The optional next step is the supplied implementation checklist at https://example.invalid/svale/checklist; it is a document to read, not a consultation booking or a product trial.” | Same optional document and reading action. “Can” expresses the offered action rather than a claim that readers actually consulted it. Supported. |
| 28 | “The team will decide on expansion after checking how the categories work for larger repairs; the trial has not yet expanded.” | “The trial has not yet expanded; the team will decide after checking how the categories work for larger repairs.” | Same current status, future deciding actor, prerequisite, and larger-repair scope. “On expansion” resolves the decision's referent from the immediately adjacent source clause. The draft does not promise expansion or state the checks have been completed. Supported. |
| 29 | “For operations managers considering their own setup” | “Write a journalistic customer case for operations managers at small housing companies.” / “The optional next step is the supplied implementation checklist at https://example.invalid/svale/checklist; it is a document to read, not a consultation booking or a product trial.” | Audience address and a hypothetical consideration, not an assertion about an actual population's behavior or intention. The audience is supplied. No finding. |
| 30 | “the supplied next step is to read Svale's implementation checklist” and the destination `https://example.invalid/svale/checklist` | “The optional next step is the supplied implementation checklist at https://example.invalid/svale/checklist; it is a document to read, not a consultation booking or a product trial.” | The link exactly preserves the supplied destination and correctly describes reading a checklist. The source's supplier publisher and supplier-named URL support identifying the checklist as Svale's. The surrounding “can consult” maintains optionality; no mandatory step, consultation, or trial is offered. Supported. |

## Person, number, and natural-gender accounting

- The draft's “its maintenance team” refers to Elm Quay Housing. “Its” is third-person singular institutional reference and grammatical neuter, without a human natural-gender claim. Source: “its own maintenance team.” Ownership and number are unchanged.
- The introduction's “the team's choices” and “its trial figures” refer to the maintenance team. The latter is a third-person singular collective possessive, without natural-gender information. Source calls it “The maintenance team” and uses “It chose”; the trial figures are supplied in Elm Quay's internal trial note. Nothing turns the collective into one human person.
- The draft's “The team” in choosing the supplier and deciding on expansion explicitly names the collective referred to by source “It” and “the team.” No sex or human natural gender is asserted.
- In quotation 1, “We” is first-person plural, “ours” first-person plural possessive, and “us” first-person plural object. Source uses the identical words. The supplied context identifies the maintenance team as the relevant group but does not enumerate its members or assign a natural gender to any of them. “Them” refers to plural categories, not people. The “evening shift” and “morning shift” remain collective shift references with no additional persons or genders.
- In quotation 2, “We” is first-person plural and “I” first-person singular. Source uses the identical words; the interview attribution establishes Lind as the first-person singular speaker. “That time” refers to time agreeing on categories, and “the next building” remains prospective. No pronoun assigns Lind a natural gender.
